Plain English — Round numbers like “1,000 days” carry no legal or administrative meaning; they are a calendar coincidence that both a government and its opposition treat as a free news hook. Mechanics — Indian governments and oppositions both maintain running day-counts of an administration’s term (100 days, 500 days, 1,000 days, and so on) specifically to have a ready-made occasion for a scorecard. Incentives — For the government, the date is a chance to control the narrative with its own numbers first; for the opposition, it is a chance to force a comparison on a day the government cannot avoid public attention. Numbers — 1,000 days is roughly 2 years 9 months — a little under a third of a typical 5-year term, making it an early-to-midpoint checkpoint, not a final verdict. S2 · The government’s own report card Civil Supplies Minister N Uttam Kumar Reddy released a document titled “1,000 Days of Welfare and Development — Telangana Report Card,” framing the period as a shift from “family rule to people’s rule” and a “restoration of democracy” after BRS’s decade in office. Plain English — A senior minister, not the Chief Minister himself, was chosen to release the document — a common practice that lets the CM stay above the specifics while a colleague carries the messaging. Mechanics — The “family rule” framing is a direct jab at BRS, which was founded and long led by the Rao family (K Chandrashekar Rao as Chief Minister, his son K T Rama Rao and daughter K Kavitha both holding senior party and government roles during BRS’s decade in power). Incentives — Releasing a self-authored report card first, before the opposition can define the narrative, is standard political sequencing — whoever publishes numbers first often gets quoted as the baseline, even if a rival immediately disputes them. Numbers — No dedicated figures in this fact; the numbers arrive in S3. S3 · The government’s headline numbers The report card cites per-capita income of Rs 4,18,931 for 2025-26 (said to be roughly 91% above the national average); farm loan waivers of up to Rs 2 lakh for about 25 lakh farming families; over Rs 36,000 crore disbursed under the Rythu Bharosa farmer-support scheme; roughly 70,000 government jobs filled; Telangana overtaking Punjab as India’s top paddy producer with 81.12 lakh tonnes procured; more than 335 crore free bus trips for women under the Mahalakshmi scheme; free electricity up to 200 units for 53 lakh families under Gruha Jyothi; and Rs 500 cooking-gas cylinders for 43 lakh families. Plain English — This is a long list of welfare-delivery numbers, each measuring how much the government spent or gave away, not independently how much better off any single family actually is. Mechanics — Every one of these numbers comes from the government’s own departments, released in the government’s own report — they are self-reported administrative statistics, not figures independently audited or verified by a third party such as the CAG at the time of release. Incentives — Big, precise-looking numbers (91% above national average; 81.12 lakh tonnes) read as more credible than round ones — a well-known messaging technique, though precision is not the same as independent verification. Numbers — Rs 36,000 crore under Rythu Bharosa alone is a very large sum — for comparison, it is close to double what the entire Raidurg land-auction programme has raised for the state government this year (roughly Rs 2,833 crore from the two most recent Raidurg sales combined, covered in earlier editions) — showing how much bigger welfare spending is than one-off land-sale revenue as a share of the state’s finances. S4 · The Moosarambagh bridge speech and the debate challenge On Monday evening (31 August), Chief Minister Revanth Reddy inaugurated a new high-level bridge over the Musi river at Moosarambagh, and used the platform to publicly challenge former Chief Minister K Chandrashekar Rao (KCR) to a floor debate in the Assembly, comparing Congress’s 1,000 days against BRS’s 10 years in power, once the Monsoon Session opens on 7 September. Plain English — The Chief Minister chose a freshly-built piece of public infrastructure as the backdrop for a direct political taunt at his predecessor. Mechanics — An Assembly “debate” challenge is more theatre than a real procedural mechanism — there is no rule that forces KCR, who is not currently attending sessions, to show up and answer; it is a rhetorical dare designed to be reported, not necessarily accepted. Incentives — By tying the challenge to a bridge inauguration, the CM gets two news events in one — a delivered-infrastructure photo-op plus a political jab — while knowing KCR is unlikely to actually appear and debate. Numbers — No new figures in this fact. S5 · The specific charges against KCR’s absence Revanth Reddy said KCR has “confined himself to his farmhouse,” has not attended a single Assembly session in the 1,000 days since losing power, drew Rs 1.24 crore in salary as a sitting MLA during that period, while the state spent about Rs 22 crore on his security and official facilities as former Chief Minister. Plain English — The CM is arguing that KCR keeps drawing a legislator’s pay and a former-CM’s security cover while doing none of the public-facing legislative work either role implies. Mechanics — In India, a sitting MLA continues to draw salary and allowances regardless of attendance (there is no automatic pay cut for absenteeism), and a former Chief Minister is entitled to a standard security and facilities package under state protocol rules — both are lawful entitlements, not misuse, which is exactly why this is a political argument about optics, not a legal or procedural violation. Incentives — Framing a legal entitlement as wasteful is a common way to make an opponent’s inaction sound like a scandal, even when nothing about it breaks any rule. Numbers — Rs 1.24 crore in salary and roughly Rs 22 crore in state-funded security/facilities over 1,000 days — these are the CM’s own claimed figures, not yet independently corroborated by an official disclosure or RTI response in the reporting reviewed, so treat them as one side’s asserted numbers. S6 · Six days of dharnas demanding KCR’s resignation Revanth Reddy called for six days of Congress-led dharnas (sit-in protests) demanding KCR’s resignation as MLA, starting Tuesday 1 September — the same day BRS was staging its own counter-campaign launch. Plain English — The ruling party is running a street-protest campaign against the very opposition leader whose party is simultaneously protesting against the ruling party — both sides are in the streets on the same days. Mechanics — A sitting MLA cannot be legally forced to resign by public protest alone; resignation demands like this function purely as pressure and messaging, similar to the “resign immediately” demand AIMIM made of expelled MLC Mirza Rahmath Baig, covered elsewhere in this edition — a request, not an enforceable outcome. Incentives — Matching the opposition’s protest calendar day-for-day denies BRS a clear run at dominating the news cycle around the 1,000-day milestone. Numbers — Six days, timed to overlap almost exactly with BRS’s own announced 2–8 September campaign window (S7). S7 · BRS’s rival chargesheet BRS working president K T Rama Rao (KTR) released a political “chargesheet” against the Congress government at Telangana Bhavan on 1 September, alleging the government has failed to fulfil even a single one of 420 promises, 13 declarations and six guarantees it originally pledged to deliver within its first 100 days in office. Plain English — BRS is arguing that Congress’s own original campaign promises, not BRS’s standards, are the yardstick Congress should be judged against — and that on that yardstick, three years on, nothing has been delivered. Mechanics — A political “chargesheet” borrows the language of a criminal charge document but carries no legal force whatsoever — it cannot be filed in any court and creates no legal liability; it is campaign material, formatted to look authoritative. Incentives — Choosing the same 1 September date as the government’s own milestone, and the same venue-style formality (a press conference at party headquarters) as a government release, is deliberate mirroring — BRS wants its document treated with the same weight as the government’s. Numbers — “Zero of 420” is BRS’s own claim and has not been independently verified fact-by-fact in the reporting available; as of this research, only the pre-event announcement of the chargesheet’s existence was confirmed, not a verified line-by-line account of its actual content on the day, so treat the “420 promises” figure as BRS’s framing, not an audited count. S8 · The week-long BRS campaign, including a land-specific protest Following the chargesheet release, BRS has planned a week-long campaign (2–8 September): constituency-level dharnas over the “six guarantees” on 2 September, the display of 420-foot-long banners and “Baaki Cards” (due/debt cards) listing unmet promises, farmer conferences across the state on 3 September covering agriculture, irrigation, power supply, urea shortages and crop insurance, and — per this edition’s earlier coverage — a protest specifically over the Section 22A prohibited-lands issue also timed to 3 September. Plain English — This is not one protest but a coordinated, multi-day statewide campaign with different themes assigned to different days, run like a mini election campaign rather than a single rally. Mechanics — Section 22A is the Telangana rule under which sub-registrars must refuse to register land on a “prohibited” list — a list that has wrongly swept up genuine private property in past months (covered in this edition’s Concept Library and earlier Deep Dives); folding a land-registration grievance into a broader “broken promises” campaign lets BRS attach a concrete, personally-felt harm (a frozen property) to an otherwise abstract political argument. Incentives — Farmer conferences and a land-registration protest both target rural and landowning voters specifically — a signal that BRS sees land and agriculture grievances as its strongest available wedge against Congress right now. Numbers — A 420-foot banner is a deliberate visual pun on the “420 promises” claim — one foot of banner per allegedly broken promise. S9 · The government’s own newspaper is not simply cheerleading Telangana Today published its own analytical piece the same evening (31 August, 6:37 PM) pushing back on parts of the government’s report card — noting that TIMS hospital projects being credited to Congress were largely built under the previous BRS government; that the Regional Ring Road has shown no progress in 30 months; that Warangal airport plans remain stalled; and that zero “Young India Integrated Residential Schools” have been built despite a promise of one per Assembly constituency. Plain English — Even before BRS’s formal chargesheet landed, at least one Telangana outlet had already independently flagged gaps between the government’s claims and the state of specific stalled projects. Mechanics — This is ordinary accountability journalism — comparing a government’s own claimed timeline against visible, checkable facts on the ground (has a road been built, has an airport plan moved, have schools opened) — not itself a partisan attack. Incentives — A same-day critical piece from a mainstream outlet, appearing independently of BRS’s own messaging, is more credible corroboration of specific gaps (RRR, Warangal airport, the residential schools) than either party’s own claims about the other. Numbers — “Zero of one-per-constituency” Young India schools, against however many of Telangana’s roughly 119 Assembly constituencies were promised one — a concrete, checkable shortfall distinct from the more rhetorical “420 promises” framing. S10 · The High Court’s land-loser question The same Telangana Today piece noted that a Telangana High Court judge, Justice N V Shravan Kumar, had separately questioned why the government found the funds to resume marriage-aid (Kalyana Lakshmi/Shaadi Mubarak-style) payments while people whose land had already been acquired for government projects were still waiting on their compensation. Plain English — A judge, hearing an unrelated case, pointedly asked why the government pays for one type of welfare promptly while people who gave up their land for public projects are left waiting to be paid what they are legally owed. Mechanics — This is a judicial observation made in passing during a hearing, not a formal court order or ruling — it carries no binding legal force and creates no enforceable deadline, but it is a rare instance of an independent, non-partisan voice raising the exact same prioritisation question both political parties have every incentive to avoid: is welfare spending being prioritised over legal compensation debts? Incentives — Neither Congress (which wants credit for welfare delivery) nor BRS (whose own government also had unresolved land-compensation cases) has an obvious incentive to spotlight this specific question, which is exactly why it is easy for it to get buried under the louder report-card-versus-chargesheet fight. Numbers — No specific compensation figure or land-loser count was available in the reporting reviewed — this is flagged as an open question, not a quantified scandal, and is worth tracking for a specific number in a future edition. Namasthe Telangana, this edition’s flagged BRS-aligned outlet, was checked for its framing of the chargesheet call but added no additional independently-verifiable facts beyond what the other outlets carried. 3 · Glossary — every term, simply 1,000 days (as a political milestone) A round-number count of a government’s time in office, with no legal significance, used as an occasion for both self-praise and opposition attack. Example: a company celebrating “10 years in business” with a sale — the number itself changes nothing, but it’s a convenient hook for a message. Report card (political) A government’s own self-graded summary of what it has achieved, published by the government itself rather than an independent body. Example: like a student writing their own school report card — informative, but you’d still want the teacher’s version too. Chargesheet (political, as used here) An opposition party’s list of a government’s alleged failures, borrowing the name of a criminal-court document but carrying no legal force. Example: a competitor’s attack ad listing everything wrong with a rival product — persuasive marketing, not a court finding. Rythu Bharosa Telangana’s scheme paying farmers a fixed per-acre cash amount each season to support cultivation costs, regardless of what crop they grow. Example: like a flat annual stipend a farmer gets just for having land under cultivation, on top of whatever they earn selling the crop. Mahalakshmi scheme A Telangana scheme letting women travel free on state-run (TGSRTC) buses. Example: a free public-transport pass, but only for women and only on government buses, not private ones. Gruha Jyothi A Telangana scheme giving eligible households free electricity up to a monthly usage cap (up to 200 units, per the report card). Example: like your electricity bill being waived entirely as long as you stay under a set usage limit each month. Per-capita income The average income per person in a region, calculated by dividing total economic output by population — a broad average that says nothing about how income is actually distributed between rich and poor. Example: if one person earns Rs 100 and nine earn Rs 0, the “per-capita income” of the group is still Rs 10 each, even though nine people have nothing. Assembly (Legislative Assembly) Telangana’s state legislature, where elected MLAs debate and pass laws and budgets. Example: like a state-level parliament; Telangana’s has about 119 elected members. MLA (Member of the Legislative Assembly) An elected representative in a state’s Assembly, representing one constituency. Example: the state-level equivalent of a Member of Parliament, but for a single state rather than the whole country. Dharna A sit-in style protest, typically peaceful, where demonstrators occupy a public space to press a demand and draw press attention. Example: a workplace sit-in, but staged in front of a government building instead of an office. Section 22A (Telangana Registration Act) The rule under which certain survey numbers are placed on a “prohibited” list that sub-registrars must refuse to register — meant to block government/temple/ceiling-surplus land sales, but prone to wrongly trapping genuine private property (fully explained in this edition’s Concept Library). Example: like a bank freezing an account by mistake because a similar account number was flagged for fraud — the freeze is real even when the underlying reason is a clerical error. CAG (Comptroller and Auditor General) India’s independent constitutional auditor of government accounts at both the central and state level — not part of any government department, and its reports are the closest thing to a neutral financial referee on claims like the ones in today’s report card. Example: like an external auditor a company is legally required to use, rather than checking its own books. High Court The highest court within a single Indian state (Telangana’s sits in Hyderabad), one level below the Supreme Court of India. Example: a state-level appellate court, roughly analogous to a US state supreme court. Land acquisition compensation The payment the government legally owes a landowner when it takes their land for a public project (a road, a bridge, an irrigation canal). Example: like a compulsory purchase in other countries — the government can take the land, but the law requires it to pay a set price for doing so, and delay in that payment is itself a legal grievance. Musi river / Musi Riverfront The river running through Hyderabad, currently the subject of a large state government redevelopment programme (the Musi Riverfront project, covered in earlier editions) that includes new bridges such as the one inaugurated at Moosarambagh. Beneath the dueling-numbers surface, the deeper forces are familiar to any state that has just changed ruling parties: a new government needs three years of delivery to look credible before the next election cycle begins to loom, while an opposition that lost power decisively needs to prove it is still relevant without the daily visibility that governing provides. Both parties are also managing internal pressures that rarely make the milestone headlines — Congress is simultaneously handling the Konda Surekha Cabinet crisis (covered elsewhere in this edition), while BRS is managing its own KCR-succession question in the background, with KTR the visible face of a party whose founder has become steadily less publicly active. What a ten-year Telangana political follower knows, that a first-time reader of today’s headlines might not: this exact report-card-versus-chargesheet pattern repeats at every major milestone in Indian state politics, and the specific numbers rarely settle anything on their own — what tends to actually move public opinion, over the following weeks, is whichever side’s claims survive contact with an independent check, such as a CAG report, a court observation, or a RERA/land-registration outcome that ordinary people can verify against their own experience. 5 · So what — stakes and consequences The government wins if its report card’s big numbers (jobs filled, farm support disbursed, free electricity and bus travel delivered) stick in public memory more than BRS’s “420 promises” framing — a battle of which side’s big number is more memorable, not necessarily which side is more accurate. BRS wins if its chargesheet, plus Telangana Today’s independent flags on stalled projects (RRR, Warangal airport, Young India schools), combine to make “undelivered” the more credible frame heading into the Assembly session and, eventually, the next election cycle. The quieter loser, so far, is whoever is still waiting on land-acquisition compensation — a group neither party’s messaging machine has any strong incentive to spotlight, and the one group a High Court judge, entirely outside the political fight, chose to raise unprompted. Watch for: (1) whether KCR actually appears for any Assembly-floor exchange after 7 September, or whether the “debate challenge” quietly drops after its news cycle passes — likelihood: KCR appearing is low, given his reported pattern of non-attendance; (2) whether BRS’s Section 22A protest on 3 September produces any concrete government response beyond the existing committee process — moderate likelihood, given the committee’s own 15-day clearance deadline lands around the same window; (3) whether any outlet or RTI response ever produces a verified land-loser compensation figure responding to Justice Shravan Kumar’s question — lower likelihood in the short term, since neither party benefits from surfacing it, but worth checking again in a future edition. What this means for you: for Hyderabad/Telangana real estate directly, the most durable thread inside today’s noise is the Section 22A protest folded into BRS’s campaign and the High Court’s land-compensation question — both point to land registration and acquisition payment delays as a live, unresolved risk category, regardless of which party’s messaging wins the news cycle. For business and investment more broadly, today’s episode is a reminder that self-reported government statistics (from either a ruling party’s report card or an opposition’s chargesheet) should be treated as advocacy until corroborated by an independent source like the CAG, a court, or a regulator such as TG-RERA. The beginner mistake here is treating either the report card or the chargesheet as the real story; the sharper read is to watch the one paragraph in Telangana Today’s independent piece and the one line from a High Court judge — the two facts in this whole episode that neither political party chose to put there themselves. 6 · The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map On the day Telangana’s Congress government completed 1,000 days in office, it published its own report card of welfare delivery, and the opposition BRS published a rival chargesheet claiming zero of 420 original promises had been kept — both released the same day, both self-authored, both unaudited at the point of release. The Chief Minister used a bridge inauguration to challenge his predecessor to a public debate that the predecessor is unlikely to accept. The one genuinely independent voice in the entire episode belonged to a High Court judge, who asked in passing why land-acquisition compensation was still unpaid while other welfare spending had resumed. 2026-09-01|ls-scams: Common land scams in India and how to protect yourself Land School — an original Deccan Ledger lesson · source & further reading: Common Land Scams in India and How to Protect Yourself — 1acre.in Key Highlights Fraud thrives where records are scattered: ~95% of RoRs are computerised, but only ~68% of cadastral maps. The deadliest scam is the LEGAL-LOOKING one: registered deeds on assigned land are void — registration proves nothing. Seven patterns cover most of the market: forged titles, restricted land, duplicate sales, PoA abuse, encroachment, benami, fake pre-launch schemes. The defence is always the same: pull the records YOURSELF — RoR, EC, prohibited list, title chain. Remote buyers and absentee owners are the favourite targets. Why India’s land market attracts so much fraud Fraud grows wherever information is scarce and checking is hard. India’s records are digitising UNEVENLY — about 95% of Records of Rights computerised but only 68% of cadastral maps, with some districts still on ageing paper — and every state runs its own system. The favourite victims: buyers unfamiliar with local revenue records, people purchasing remotely, and plots whose owners are absent or unaware something is being sold in their name. The most devastating one: restricted land sold as normal Certain land legally CANNOT be freely sold: government-assigned land, tribal land, ceiling-surplus land, endowment (temple) land, forest land. The scam: a legitimate-looking registered document, payment made, registration completed — and years or decades later the government reclaims the land because it was assigned all along. Buyer loses land, money and everything built on it. The legal trap: the prohibited-list mechanism (Section 22-A) only BLOCKS registration of parcels actually on the Collector’s list — unlisted assigned parcels register fine — but the transfer-ban law voids the sale regardless of what any registrar accepted. So: check the prohibited register AND the revenue record’s remarks, always. Seven scams to know 1) Title fraud and forged documents — the most widespread: a fraudster forges papers, poses as owner or PoA holder, sells land that is not theirs; forged paper carries zero legal weight, which is why the CHAIN matters more than the current deed. 2) Restricted-land sales — as above. 3) Duplicate sales — one plot sold to two or more buyers, exploiting slow registration; not a pure first-to-register race (a deed relates back to its execution date under Section 47), but the genuinely prior sale usually prevails and everyone else litigates. 4) PoA abuse — forged, expired or revoked PoAs used to sell without the owner’s knowledge; an unregistered PoA, or one not clearly authorising sale, is a warning. 5) Encroachment folded in — the boundary shown quietly includes government or neighbouring land; good title to part, nothing on the rest; a boundary survey catches it. 6) Benami deals — property in someone else’s name to hide the real buyer; illegal under the 2016 Benami law, with confiscation and up to seven years’ rigorous imprisonment. 7) Fake pre-launch schemes — units sold in unapproved projects with assured-return promises backed by post-dated cheques that bounce; RERA bars selling before registration, so a pre-launch pitch WITHOUT a RERA number is the tell. Definition — Benami transaction: a purchase held in a name-lender’s name while someone else pays and controls it. Since the 2016 amendment the property can be confiscated outright — buyer-side participation is itself the crime. Red flags and what they mean Warning sign What it usually means What to do Price well below market Defect the seller knows and you don’t Slow down; the discount IS the disclosure Pressure to close fast Verification window being shortened deliberately Never pay before checks complete Seller supplies all documents, resists your own EC pull Papers may be curated or forged Pull EC and RoR yourself from official sources Sale via PoA, owner unreachable Possible PoA abuse or a dead/unaware principal Meet or video-verify the owner; check PoA registration “Registration will fix everything” Confusing registration with valid title Remember: void transfers register too No RERA number on a project pitch Unapproved / pre-launch scheme Verify on the state RERA portal before any token Documents to check before any purchase ☐ Title + sale deed — seller’s name matches the record; chain traced 30 years. ☐ Record of Rights — owner, classification, mutation history, restriction remarks. ☐ EC — pulled by YOU from the sub-registrar; never the seller’s copy. ☐ Land use / conversion — classification confirmed; conversion completed if it was agricultural. ☐ Mutation — updated, no restriction notes. ☐ Tax receipts — dues attach to the LAND, not the old owner. ☐ RERA — verified on the portal for any plotted or builder project. ☐ PoA, if involved — authorises sale, registered where required, traceable to the real owner. What maps can and cannot catch Survey-number maps, master-plan overlays and satellite imagery catch boundary and zoning mismatches — whether the parcel’s ground reality matches the deed, and whether it sits in a restricted zone — before a site visit. They cannot read a title chain, tell a forged deed from a genuine one, or check the prohibited list. That work stays with the sub-registrar’s records and a revenue-law advocate. Quick answers (FAQ) Most common scam? Title fraud with forged documents. How do I know if land has transfer restrictions? RoR remarks + the state’s prohibited-property register. Can I buy through a PoA? Yes, with independent verification of the PoA and the principal — PoA sales are not inherently illegitimate. What if I unknowingly bought restricted land? The transfer is void; get a revenue advocate immediately. Is RERA-registered land always safe? Safer — but RERA checks the project, not the title chain; do both. How to report fraud? Police complaint (EOW for large frauds) + civil suit; registration of a case does not undo the transfer, so prevention is the real remedy. Bottom line Nearly every land scam succeeds at the same moment: when the buyer accepts someone else’s paperwork instead of pulling their own. RoR, EC, prohibited list, 30-year chain, boundary survey — five self-service checks defeat all seven scams. For you: Your buyers fear exactly this list — which makes it your marketing. A venture that publishes its own verification file (chain, EC, prohibited-list clearance, DTCP approval) sells trust the unorganised market cannot. Internally: rule — no landowner conversation advances until the RoR and prohibited-list check are done, however warm the introduction. The Encumbrance Certificate, pulled for 15–30 years, is the first filter for hidden loans and old claims. eCourts and the NJDG let you search pending cases free — but a wrong spelling can hide the case. Lis pendens binds a new buyer to a pending case’s outcome even if nobody told them it existed. Revenue-court disputes and old village claims are often NOT online — a physical visit still counts. What checking for disputes actually means There is a difference between a title that LOOKS fine and one that has been CHECKED. Land carries history the deed never shows: an old inheritance quarrel, a boundary shifted after a family split, a loan never cleared. A litigation check confirms — through independent sources, never the seller’s word — that none of this is unresolved. Two different searches get confused: the EC tracks registered financial claims; a court search tracks live litigation. A property can be clean on one and dirty on the other. What a proper check covers Encumbrance history — loans, mortgages, claims, from the SRO. Court cases — anything involving the owner or the property, via eCourts and the NJDG. Ownership and survey records — mutation entries cross-checked against the deed. Unrecorded local disputes — boundary and revenue matters not yet digital. The neighbours — who usually know about a fight before any court does. Why the check must happen before you pay anything Land fights make up a striking share of India’s pending civil cases, tracing to a few causes: contested inheritance, forged papers, unclear titles, encroachment. A seller with a pending case usually will not mention it. The check matters at three moments: before the offer, before any advance, and before registration — each later stage makes a discovered defect more expensive. Definition — Lis pendens: “suit pending”. Once litigation over land is on foot, whoever buys the land inherits the case’s outcome — knowledge or ignorance makes no difference. The law assumes you searched. Start with the Encumbrance Certificate Ask for at least 15 years, ideally 30 — a spotless five-year EC says nothing about a fifteen-year-old dispute that never resolved. Read it for court attachments, unreleased liens, and windows where entries abruptly stop; a gap is a question, not a quirk. Then search eCourts and the NJDG Both portals cover District and High Courts, searchable by party name, case number or type — free. Search the owner’s name in every reasonable variation (initials, spellings), the FAMILY’S names, and past owners’ names from the chain. A nil result under one spelling proves only that spelling. Example: A buyer near Shamshabad stopped at a clean EC. The seller’s sister’s partition suit was two minutes away on eCourts — under HER name. The court notice arrived after his registration; lis pendens did the rest. Red flags — what they usually mean, what to do Red flag What it usually means What to do EC entries suddenly stop A dispute or transaction may have been kept off the record Ask the SRO for a written explanation of the gap eCourts returns nothing at all The case may sit under a name variant Re-search with initials and past owners’ names Seller resists the full-period EC Possibly avoiding an older entry Insist on the 15–30 year window — non-negotiable Neighbours mention a fight the seller did not Local knowledge runs ahead of filings Visit the tahsildar; investigate before any advance Title changed hands fast and often Rapid resales can be laundering a defect Trace and check each prior owner in the chain The physical checks documents cannot replace Revenue-court records — at the tahsildar or sub-divisional office — are mostly not digitised; someone must go and look. Neighbours help more than expected. For anything beyond a small purchase, a lawyer running the full search is cheap against the alternative. Pre-purchase checklist ☐ EC for 15–30 years. ☐ eCourts + NJDG searched under every reasonable name variation. ☐ Ownership and survey details cross-checked on the state portal. ☐ SRO and revenue office visited for what is not online. ☐ Neighbours asked about disputes and boundaries. ☐ Lawyer’s full search before any advance. Quick answers (FAQ) Can I search property litigation online free? Yes — eCourts and NJDG. Do all disputes show there? No — revenue matters and fresh village fights often exist offline first. What if I unknowingly buy disputed land? Lis pendens binds you to the outcome; your recourse is against the seller — which is why the check precedes the money. How far back should the EC go? 30 years where possible; 15 as the floor. Bottom line Disputes rarely announce themselves; they sit in old entries and filings the seller has no reason to mention. A few hours across the EC, eCourts and one village visit cost almost nothing against untangling a case later. It does not prove ownership — that is the title deed’s job. The EC validates; it does not replace. Its blind spot is everything unregistered: private loans, informal partitions, unregistered agreements, most litigation. A “clean” (Nil) EC can simply mean the search ran on the wrong number or window. Read it WITH the title chain and the ground — alone, it leaves gaps a buyer can walk straight into. What an EC actually shows A government-issued log from the SRO of every registered event on the property in your chosen period: sales, mortgages, gifts, releases, leases — with owners as they appear in deeds, the property description, and document numbers and dates for each entry. It has become India’s shorthand for title verification: banks refuse loans without a clear one; lawyers start every search here. Why an EC is not proof of ownership The single most important sentence in this lesson: the EC shows registered TRANSACTION history; OWNERSHIP is proved by the title deed and the chain behind it. Think of the EC as the property’s credit report — what happened on record — not its birth certificate. What the EC misses entirely Only registered documents enter it. So these never appear: oral family settlements; informal partitions between siblings; unregistered agreements to sell; private loans through unregistered mortgages — including the very common deposit-of-title-deeds mortgage with a bank; and court cases, unless officially recorded at the SRO. Definition — Equitable mortgage (deposit of title deeds): a loan created by handing the original deeds to a lender. No registration, no EC entry — which is why sighting the ORIGINALS is a due-diligence step no certificate replaces. Example: Spotless 30-year EC; seller’s originals “with his brother”. More often than not the originals are with a bank, against a loan the EC cannot see. The absence of originals is the loudest entry the EC never prints. EC vs the other property documents Document What it proves What it does NOT prove Encumbrance Certificate Registered transaction/liability history for a period Ownership; unregistered deals; undisclosed litigation Title / sale deed Legal ownership and its transfer to the holder Freedom from hidden liabilities — the EC’s job Mutation certificate The property’s entry in revenue/tax records Legal ownership — mutation is a tax record Property tax receipts Taxes paid; possession exercised Clear title or absence of disputes The classic misreadings The mortgage with no release deed — the property may still be pledged; if the loan was never cleared the lender’s rights survive your purchase. The Nil EC celebrated too early — Form 16 (nil) may mean genuinely clean, or wrong survey number, or wrong classification; a clean result is a prompt to verify WHY it is clean, against pahani / extract / patta. The unexplained jump — ownership hopping from one name to a third with no visible link; that missing link is precisely what a careful read catches. Definition — Form 15 / Form 16: the two faces of an EC in the southern states: Form 15 lists the registered entries found; Form 16 is the nil-encumbrance certificate saying the search found nothing in the window. What to check alongside the EC The sale deed and title chain; mutation entries; tax receipts; a physical survey against documented boundaries; and an independent litigation check through court records. Window: minimum 13 years, ideally 30 — the certificate only reflects the period actually searched. It is a question wearing good news’s clothes: why is it clean? Bottom line The EC is a necessary check, never a complete one — what was registered, not who owns. Pair it with the chain, the mutation record and the ground, and its silences stop being traps. Incentives — A ticket demand delivered as a public attack, rather than through internal party channels, is a pressure tactic: it forces the party to either concede the seat publicly (rewarding the confrontation) or discipline the family publicly (creating a martyr narrative) — there was no quiet third option once the remarks were public. Numbers — The ₹200-crore figure in the land-deal allegation was not new on 19 August — BRS working president K.T. Rama Rao had first raised a nearly identical figure on 11 August, over a different, TDP-adjacent controversy (see F4 dossier on Tesseract Advanced Systems); Sushmitha’s remarks amplified an existing opposition talking point rather than introducing a new allegation. F4 · Surekha’s own reaction after being dropped Minutes after her removal, Surekha told reporters she was “not at all at fault,” that she should not be held responsible for her adult, independent daughter’s remarks, that no one had consulted her before the decision, and that Revanth Reddy had “blackmailed” the Congress leadership by threatening to resign if she were not removed; she separately alleged a conspiracy involving the Chief Minister’s brothers, Rajya Sabha MP Vem Narender Reddy, and Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivasa Reddy, and said she would remain in the Congress party and continue as Warangal East MLA. Plain English — She refused to accept blame, accused the Chief Minister of strong-arming his own party over her removal, and said despite everything she is staying put in Congress rather than quitting or defecting. Mechanics — Staying in the party while publicly attacking its leadership is a deliberate middle path — it keeps her Warangal East Assembly seat and her formal Congress membership intact (an MLA does not lose their seat by losing a ministership) while keeping every grievance on the public record. Incentives — A sacked minister with nothing left to lose inside the government has every incentive to name names publicly — unlike a minister still in office, she now faces no departmental consequence for speaking freely, which is exactly what her conspiracy allegation does. Numbers — Not applicable; this fact is entirely about public statements, not measurable figures. F5 · The same-day, separate action against G. Chinna Reddy Hours before or alongside Surekha’s removal, the Congress high command also rescinded G. Chinna Reddy’s appointment as Telangana State Planning Board Vice-Chairman, over remarks he made against the party leadership and Wanaparthy MLA T. Megha Reddy at a Gopalpet mandal Congress office inauguration on 16 August; Telangana State Women’s Commission Chairperson Gadwal Vijayalakshmi was named his successor with immediate effect. Incentives — Bundling two unrelated disciplinary cases into one news cycle is cheaper for a party’s image than letting them surface as two separate bad-news days — a pattern this paper’s Concept Library already named “simultaneous disciplinary bundling” after an earlier reshuffle round. Numbers — Chinna Reddy’s remarks (16 August) preceded Sushmitha’s (19 August) by three days, yet both cases concluded on the same 3 September date — suggesting the party timed the resolution to its own internal calendar, not to either individual controversy’s own timeline. Incentives — Blaming a named rival rather than the leadership itself lets Chinna Reddy stay inside the party’s good graces with the top leadership while still publicly venting — a more cautious version of the same playbook Surekha used, aimed one rung lower down the hierarchy. Plain English — The main opposition party is using the sacking to attack Congress on two fronts at once: alleged corruption, and how it treats its senior women leaders. Mechanics — An opposition party has no obligation to be consistent about WHY it is criticising a rival’s internal decision — here BJP is simultaneously implying the underlying land-deal allegation has merit AND that Surekha was treated unfairly, two framings that would normally be in tension, but both serve the single goal of damaging Congress’s image. Mechanics — Portfolios do not sit empty in practice — the Chief Minister typically retains or temporarily reassigns a vacated department to another sitting minister “on additional charge” until a formal reshuffle settles the question permanently. Incentives — Leaving the assignment open rather than rushing a temporary fix gives Revanth Reddy maximum flexibility to fold this decision into the larger, already-anticipated Cabinet expansion, rather than making two separate announcements. No outlet in this sweep independently investigated whether the Tesseract land allotment was in fact irregular — every account of it traces back to BRS’s own political messaging, a gap this deep dive flags rather than fills. 3 · Glossary — every term, simply Council of Ministers The full team of ministers who run a state government alongside the Chief Minister — in India, its members legally hold office “during the pleasure of the Governor,” but that pleasure is exercised, by convention, entirely on the sitting Chief Minister’s advice. Dropping a minister Removing someone from the Council of Ministers without any court process or vote — simply a CM’s recommendation and a Governor’s formal approval, which is why it can happen, as here, within a single day. AICC (All India Congress Committee) The Indian National Congress’s national organisational body, headed by its president (currently Mallikarjun Kharge) — the party’s highest authority above any individual state unit. TPCC (Telangana Pradesh Congress Committee) The Congress party’s Telangana state unit, distinct from the state government itself — its Disciplinary Committee is the body that issued the show-cause notices at the centre of this story. AICC in-charge (state) A senior national Congress leader (currently Meenakshi Natarajan for Telangana) appointed to oversee a state unit’s affairs and report back to the party president — effectively Delhi’s eyes and ears inside a state party. Show-cause notice A formal internal party letter demanding a written explanation for specific conduct, before any disciplinary decision is made — more a warning shot than a punishment, though it can lead to one. Disciplinary Committee (party) A state party unit’s own internal panel, here chaired by MP Dr Mallu Ravi, that investigates a member’s conduct and recommends — but does not itself impose — punishment. State Planning Board A state-government advisory body that helps plan development priorities and spending across departments and districts; its Vice-Chairman post carries Cabinet-Minister-equivalent protocol rank, though it is not itself a Council of Ministers post and does not need the Governor’s sign-off to fill or vacate. Additional charge Temporarily assigning a vacated department to an existing minister on top of their own portfolio, until a permanent replacement is named — the likely near-term fate of Surekha’s Forest, Environment and Endowments portfolios. Article 164(1A) (Cabinet size ceiling) The constitutional provision capping any state’s Council of Ministers, including the Chief Minister, at 15% of the state Legislative Assembly’s total membership — the hard limit any Telangana Cabinet expansion has to work within. Endowments Department The state department (one of the two Surekha held) responsible for administering land and assets belonging to Hindu temples and other religious endowments — a department whose land dealings are a recurring source of political controversy across Indian states. Forest clearance Government permission required before forest land can be diverted to any non-forest use (roads, mining, real estate-adjacent infrastructure); the Forest Minister’s office is a key node in this approval chain — another reason this portfolio’s vacancy matters beyond politics. Shell company A company that exists mostly on paper, with little or no real staff, operations or revenue — the specific allegation levelled against Tesseract Advanced Systems, based on its reported ₹1-lakh paid-up capital and lack of employees. Lokayukta A state-level anti-corruption ombudsman empowered to investigate allegations against public officials — the body BRS says it will approach, alongside the Governor, over the Tesseract land allotment. 4 · The backstory — how we got here When What 7 Dec 2023 Revanth Reddy’s Cabinet is sworn in; Konda Surekha becomes Minister for Forest, Environment & Endowments. 2024 Surekha draws controversy for remarks linking KTR to the Samantha Ruth Prabhu–Naga Chaitanya divorce, later withdraws the comments — an earlier sign of her habit of unfiltered public remarks. 11 Aug 2026 KTR/BRS first allege the Tesseract Advanced Systems land deal, worth about ₹200 crore, linked to the Chief Minister’s brother. 16 Aug 2026 G. The deeper forces here run well beyond one family’s remarks. Konda Surekha had, by her own account, already been losing internal turf battles before this crisis broke — sidelined, she said, on tender decisions around the Samakka Saralamma Jathara (a major state-supported religious fair that falls under her own Endowments-adjacent responsibilities) and outmanoeuvred by Revenue Minister Ponguleti Srinivasa Reddy on a Medaram-linked works contract. A party leadership managing multiple ambitious ministers, competing camps, and a Cabinet already three seats short of full strength had every structural reason to use a public controversy as the occasion to also resolve an unrelated case (Chinna Reddy’s) it had been sitting on for weeks. What a ten-year follower of Telangana Congress politics knows, that a first-time reader does not: intra-party discipline cases in this government rarely move in isolation — they cluster around reshuffle windows, because resolving several at once is cheaper in headlines than resolving them one at a time. The BC-leader angle (Surekha, and now the BC names doing the reshuffle rounds as Cabinet-expansion aspirants) is also a running thread across this paper’s recent coverage, not a one-off; watch whether the eventual three new inductees include another BC leader, which would suggest the party is deliberately managing this exact optics problem rather than reacting to it case by case. 5 · So what — stakes and consequences Chief Minister Revanth Reddy wins in the short term: the public disciplinary crisis is formally closed, and he demonstrated he can remove a sitting minister without a party revolt. Konda Surekha loses her ministership and the institutional power that came with it, but keeps her Assembly seat and party membership — a survivable, if diminished, outcome. G. Chinna Reddy loses a state appointment over an unrelated matter, collateral to the timing of Surekha’s case. The clearest loser, at least for now, is clarity itself: two land-relevant portfolios (Forest, Endowments) currently have no confirmed minister, at exactly the moment this paper’s other stories today (the HMDA Inmulnarva auction, the ongoing Section 22A relief push) show how much land administration in Telangana is actively in motion. What this means for you: (a) For Hyderabad/Telangana real estate specifically — any file currently sitting with Forest or Endowments (a forest-diversion clearance, an endowment/wakf-adjacent land question) has no confirmed decision-maker right now; budget for delay until a successor, even on additional charge, is named, and watch this paper for that name the moment it is reported. (b) For business/investment generally — a state government that can resolve two unrelated internal-discipline cases in a single news cycle, cleanly and without visible internal revolt, is signalling institutional control even while under opposition pressure on multiple fronts (the 22A crisis, the CAG fiscal report, this land-deal allegation) — a useful, if imperfect, read on political stability for anyone weighing longer-horizon investment in the state. The beginner mistake is treating this as pure political gossip with no bearing on your business; the sharper read is that ministerial reshuffles are exactly when land-portfolio decision-makers change, and tracking WHO holds WHICH file, in real time, is a genuinely useful due-diligence habit for a plotting developer, not an idle political hobby. 6 · The 20% that gives you 100% — your keep-forever map On 3 September, Chief Minister Revanth Reddy sacked Forest, Environment & Endowments Minister Konda Surekha, with the Governor’s same-day approval, after her daughter’s 19 August public attack on him — which itself echoed an existing BRS allegation about a ₹200-crore government land deal linked to the CM’s brother — triggered a party disciplinary process that ended with Surekha appealing directly to the national Congress president and losing anyway. The same day, in an unrelated case, G. Chinna Reddy lost his Planning Board Vice-Chairman post too, and Cabinet-expansion talk (three open berths) is now live. What Lal Dora and Abadi Deh actually mean Around 1908, colonial revenue officers drew a literal red line — lal dora — on village maps, separating the lived-in area from the surrounding farmland, and revenue departments were told to maintain that distinction ever after. Abadi or Abadi Deh is the same zone described from the revenue-record side: the village habitation area itself. Whatever a document calls it, both point at one category — village residential space running on a different rulebook from both farmland and planned urban colonies. Why these areas sit outside normal property rules The defining feature: lal dora areas were historically EXEMPT from building and zoning regulations — houses rose for generations without permits or codes. So a decades-old house inside the line is not automatically an illegal structure; it operates under a genuinely different, older framework. That is meaningfully different from unauthorised construction in a regular colony — even though the two can look identical from the street. The real trade-off As cities swallowed villages, these pockets became affordable islands beside prime urban zones — Delhi’s Chhatarpur and Munirka belts are the famous examples; Hyderabad’s old village cores inside GHMC are the local cousins. The attraction is price and position. The pitfalls run equally deep: ownership is typically NOT formally documented, structures lack sanction, and the legal safeguards a normal buyer expects — clean registration, bank finance, municipal recourse — thin out or vanish. Example: Two plots on the same road: the titled one at ₹60,000/sq yd, the abadi one at ₹35,000. The ₹25,000 gap is the market pricing three questions — can ownership be proven, can a plan be sanctioned, can your eventual buyer get a loan? The discount is not a bargain; it is a price tag on missing paper. Can you actually buy, sell and register this land? Yes — conditionally, not like a standard transaction. The seller needs verifiable proof of ownership through inheritance records, mutation, or prior registered transfers; some jurisdictions require approval from the tahsildar, SDM or municipal authority before the sale; and the property must be free of litigation and encroachment claims. Registration follows the same conditional path — possible under the state’s village-land policies, never automatic. In practice, sales within the family or village move smoothly; sales to outside third parties — especially where urban expansion looms — draw far more scrutiny. Red flags Broken ownership chains — generations of informal transfers leave gaps that surface exactly when you try to resell. No approved building plans — any construction dispute loses its normal municipal resolution path. Thin municipal services — affecting livability and resale both. Survey-scheme errors — where new village-survey programmes (like SVAMITVA property cards) apply, an uncorrected draft entry can complicate mutation, inheritance and sale. Definition — SVAMITVA: a central scheme using drone surveys to map village habitation areas and issue property cards — the first formal ownership paper many abadi properties have ever had. Where it has run, the card is a key verification document; where the draft entry is wrong, fixing it comes before buying. Lal Dora property vs regular freehold Aspect Lal Dora / Abadi property Regular freehold property What it is Long-standing village habitation under revenue records Formally registered under standard municipal and land law Source of ownership Possession + informal transfer history; revenue records A clear registered title chain via the SRO Building rules Historic exemption; newer overlays vary Full sanction regime applies Best suited to Buyers prioritising low entry cost and location over certainty Buyers prioritising finance-ability and resale liquidity True cost Cheap upfront; hidden cost in blocked loans and resale friction Full market price; fewer downstream complications Is it a reliable investment? That constraint follows the property forever: your future buyer faces the same wall, which caps resale liquidity. The bull case some investors run — regularisation catching up and prices converging with authorised areas — is a bet on future POLICY, not a guaranteed outcome. Definition — Mutation (dakhil kharij / khata transfer / patta transfer): the state updating its own ledger of who holds the land — the bridge between the registered deed and the revenue record. Registration changes OWNERSHIP; mutation changes the government’s BOOKS. What the process verifies Not a rubber stamp. The reviewing officer checks that the applicant is the rightful new owner based on a valid transfer document — sale deed, gift deed, or inheritance record — and cross-checks the property’s survey number, area and boundaries against the existing revenue record. One heir applying while others exist? Expect to produce their no-objection letters and an indemnity bond. Why it matters An unmutated register keeps showing the OLD owner though the sale is legally complete. Consequences compound: tax bills keep going to the previous owner while unpaid dues attach to the LAND, not the person; banks reject loans because mutation status is a basic ownership check; resale gets harder because the next buyer’s advocate flags the mismatch instantly; and heir disputes drag for years while land sits under a deceased owner’s name. Example: A buyer purchases in 2018, never mutates. In 2024 a tax-arrears notice arrives — the previous owner’s unpaid dues, now attached to the land. Then the bank declines a mortgage: “record shows a different owner”. Two problems, one skipped application that would have taken a few weeks in 2018. When to apply Immediately after any transaction — some states now run online or even automated mutation for straightforward transfers, others still take manual applications at the revenue office. The two classic delays: assuming the sale deed alone is enough, and inherited land sitting unmutated across a generation. Buying land that moved informally within a family? Ask whether mutation was completed at EACH step, not just the latest. Buying? Check mutation status first The seller-vs-record match is precisely the check that fails on an unmutated parcel — and it is checkable from outside (Dharani in Telangana shows the current pattadar).
